name: PT Rig Tenders Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Rig Tenders Indonesia: a coal-fleet charter book priced below its own cash
frontmatter.summary: RIGS charters tugs and barges to Indonesian coal producers and trades below the cash and securities on its balance sheet, so the operating fleet is free. We rate BUY with a target of Rp1,461, an expected return of 143.5%, on a through-cycle FCFF valuation that reproduces the last actual year and assumes no dividend.
thesis: The market capitalisation of IDR365.5bn is smaller than the IDR504.8bn of cash, time deposits and bonds at the last balance-sheet date, so the charter business is valued at less than nothing.
The fleet still earns: FY2026 EBITDA was IDR132.4bn in a year when revenue fell to IDR291.1bn, and free cash flow to the firm was IDR120.5bn after dry-dock capex [S6, F7, F9].
The first quarter of the new fiscal year confirms the demand trough rather than a collapse: revenue of IDR69.8bn, down from the prior-year quarter, and gross profit of IDR13.5bn [S8, F20, F21].
Costs are mostly fixed in rupiah and the balance sheet carries no debt that matters, so a lower coal charter market hits revenue and margin without threatening solvency [S6 p.10].
The base case pays no dividend: the consolidated unappropriated balance is in deficit and every AGM since the last distribution has retained earnings [S6 p.10, S10 p.80].
The catalyst is the annual meeting on 10 November 2026, which decides the use of FY2026 profit and a change of business classification [S5].

catalysts.event: Annual general meeting: approval of FY2026 accounts, use of FY2026 profit, change of business classification and board changes
Half-year FY2027 results (quarter to 31 December 2026), the first full test of the charter-book trough

blocks.text: We initiate Rig Tenders Indonesia (RIGS) at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp1,461, 143.5% above the Rp600 price. The company owns and charters tugs, flat-top barges and self-discharging barges to Indonesian thermal-coal producers and traders, and it has ended up with a balance sheet that is worth more than the equity market value. At the last balance-sheet date the group held IDR504.8bn of cash, time deposits and bonds against IDR0.3bn of finance-lease debt [S6 p.10, S8 p.4]. The market capitalisation is IDR365.5bn [S0]. The DCF in this note values the operating business at IDR403.9bn enterprise value and adds the net cash, producing a fundamental value of Rp1,491 per share before the liquidity discount; the probability-weighted scenario value is Rp1,826, and the house target applies a 20.0% discount for a free float of 17.5% [S0].

The variant view is not that coal is about to boom. It is that the equity price now implies a negative value for a fleet that generated IDR132.4bn of EBITDA and IDR120.5bn of free cash flow to the firm in FY2026, a year in which revenue fell to IDR291.1bn from IDR365.9bn [S6, F1, F2, F7, F9]. Our base case does not assume a recovery to the FY2025 charter book; it reproduces the depressed FY2026 economics, holds the gross margin at the level the latest quarter delivered, and lets the coal deck's own long-run price set the terminal year.

Two things move the value. First, the size and deployment of the cash pile: the DCF credits it at face value, and every rupiah returned or invested above the risk-free rate adds to the equity value. Second, the charter book: the three largest customers supplied 100.0% of gross revenue in FY2026 and the largest alone 41.6%, so a single contract loss is a step change in the operating value [S6 p.74].

Indonesian coal logistics is a volume business: barges and tugs move coal from mine
stockpiles down rivers and along the coast to transhipment points and mother vessels.
Charter rates follow coal export volumes and the balance of barge supply, not the coal
price itself, which is why a shipper can earn a stable spread while the coal price moves.
RIGS is a small, family-controlled issuer with a long operating history and a thin free
float, and its shares trade infrequently relative to the larger coal names.

RIGS is an Indonesian shipping company whose consolidated business is the charter of vessels and accommodation work barges to offshore oil and gas companies and coal transportation services; it began commercial operations in 1974 and is domiciled in Jakarta [S6 p.15]. The group reports a single operating segment, coal transportation services, and a single geographical segment, Indonesia [S6 p.70]. The fleet consists of 63 flat-top and self-discharging barges used in port and coastal coal transport [S4], and the company describes its services as transporting ships in port and transportation and delivery for coal customers [S4].

Revenue is charter and freight income recognised when the service is delivered. The customer base is concentrated by design: the three largest customers represented 100.0% of gross revenue in FY2026, and the largest customer alone accounted for 41.6%, up from a lower share in FY2025 [S6 p.74]. The named customers in the revenue note are PT Arutmin Indonesia, PT Maritim Barito Perkasa and PT Pelayaran Kartika Samudra Adijaya, which contributed IDR121.0bn, IDR96.5bn and IDR73.6bn of revenue respectively in FY2026 [S6 p.57]. All three are third parties to the group [S6 p.47]. The FY2026 decline was concentrated in two of them: Kartika and Maritim Barito both fell sharply, while Arutmin was broadly stable [S6, F13-F15]. That pattern matters for the forecast: the largest customer did not leave, but two mid-sized charter programmes were cut.

The group structure is simple. PT Rig Tenders Indonesia Tbk is the listed parent and has one subsidiary; the ultimate parent is PT Surya Indah Muara Pantai ("SIMP"), which held 80.5% of the shares when the controlling block was acquired from Scomi Marine [S10 p.18, S6 p.15]. The company's own shareholder page records SIMP at 80.5% with the remainder held by the public as of June 2023 [S9]. The data pack records a free float of 17.5% and insider ownership of 82.2% at the price date [S0]. The board at 30 June 2026 comprised President Commissioner Hadi Sunarto, Commissioner Ratna Sari Suhartono, Independent Commissioner Mikrowa Kirana, and a Board of Directors led by President Director Kartika Hadi [S6 p.15]. The annual meeting called for 10 November 2026 will ask shareholders to change the company's business classification to the current KBLI standard and to change the composition of the boards, without naming candidates in the notice [S5].

The operating model is asset-heavy and contract-driven. Vessels are carried at IDR328.7bn, which the auditor identifies as roughly a third of total assets and the main driver of charter cash flows [S6 p.5]. Dry-docking and vessel depreciation sit inside cost of revenue, so the gross margin carries the fleet's maintenance cycle rather than hiding it below the line [S6 p.52]. Capital expenditure was IDR49.6bn in FY2026 after IDR87.2bn in FY2025 [S6, F9, F10], and the first quarter of FY2027 alone absorbed capex equal to a large share of its quarterly revenue [S8 p.7]. The company is a challenger in a fragmented barge market rather than a price-setter; its edge is customer tenure and the ability to operate a mixed flat-top and self-discharging fleet, not scale.

The controlling shareholder acquired the block from a Malaysian marine-services group,
and the company has since run as a standalone Indonesian shipowner. Coal logistics
contracts are typically annual or multi-year time charters with fuel and port costs
allocated between owner and charterer, which is why the customer relationship and the
vessel specification matter more than the spot coal price.

RIGS sells capacity into the Indonesian thermal-coal export chain. The industry's volume driver is coal shipped out of Kalimantan and Sumatra to regional buyers, and its price driver for the shipper is the charter rate per tonne or per day, which rises and falls with export volumes and the supply of barges. The company itself frames the outlook through coal prices: "The prospect of future coal price is positive, driven by demand in the regional market" [S4]. We do not take that as a forecast. The reviewed coal deck has Newcastle at US$150/t spot, US$118/t for FY2027E and US$105/t in the long run, and the Indonesian reference HBA at US$127/t spot against US$112/t for FY2027E [deck]. The deck therefore embeds a lower coal price than spot in every explicit forecast year, which is the right setting for a shipper whose customers plan volumes off a normalised price rather than a spike. The deck is contextual rather than a mechanical revenue driver: RIGS buys no coal, so there is no coal-linked cost line to wire and the coal price cannot reach the cost base [S6 p.57]. We also do not capitalise a spot-holding Newcastle scenario: the base case grows revenue at 2.0% in the explicit years and 2.5% in perpetuity, so it assumes no charter-rate re-rating above the deck's long-run marker. A return to spot coal prices is upside to the bull case, not a base-case input [deck].

The industry card for commodity cyclicals asks for a through-cycle price, a cost-curve position, reserve life and a dividend-capacity cross-check. Most of that frame does not transfer to a vessel owner. RIGS has no reserves and no royalty obligation: it buys no coal, so the Newcastle and HBA series price its customers' product, not its own [S6 p.57]. The coal cycle reaches the P&L through charter demand and utilisation, which we carry in revenue growth, and through bunker fuel, which is the one direct commodity cost [S6, F24]. The company discloses that fuel risk is managed by contract: either the customer provides the fuel, or the rate charged is adjusted to current fuel prices for the service period [S6 p.71]. We model that as full pass-through, which is why we do not model a fuel-driven margin recovery or collapse; the observed FY2026 margin compression came from lower charter volume spread over a fixed cost base, not from an unhedged bunker bet.

Competitive positioning is weak on paper and adequate in practice. The five forces are unfavourable at the buyer gate: three customers take all of the revenue, the largest takes 41.6%, and coal producers can and do switch barge capacity between owners [S6 p.74, F13-F15]. Rivalry is high because the asset is standardised and the market has many small owners; barriers to entry are capital and permits rather than technology. Supplier power sits with fuel and crew, and the group is small enough that a single dry-dock slip can move a quarter's revenue. Regulation is a two-sided force: the domestic-shipping final tax of 1.2% of gross revenue is a low, simple charge booked in operating expenses [S6 p.30], while the coal-export regime, the DMO price cap and the royalty schedule shape the customers' margins and therefore their willingness to charter [deck]. The moat, such as it is, is the customer relationship and the fleet's self-discharging capability, which lets a producer unload without dedicated port gear. We would not pay for a moat beyond the book value of the vessels.

The industry deck's macro tilt is cautious. The firm brief carries a balance-of-payments pressure stance, a neutral thermal-coal view and a neutral commodity bloc, with USD/IDR at Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E against a spot of Rp18,132/USD, and Brent at US$84.0/bbl against a spot of US$104/bbl [deck]. For RIGS the FX channel is small: almost all receipts and expenditures are in rupiah, and the group does not hedge because its exposure is immaterial [S6 p.71]. The Brent channel is real but contained, and contractual pass-through neutralises it: oil and lubricants were IDR35.1bn of FY2026 cost of revenue, about 15.9% of the cost base, but the group either has the customer supply the fuel or adjusts the rate to current fuel prices [S6, F24, p.71]. A lower Brent deck is therefore close to neutral for the gross margin, not a thesis in itself.

The Indonesian barge market is regional and relationship-driven. Owners compete on
availability, loading speed and safety record; producers value reliability during the
monsoon and at peak export months. Scale helps with dry-dock scheduling and crew
retention but does not confer pricing power, because a charterer can usually re-let
tonnage. Consolidation among coal producers has gradually shifted bargaining power to
the buyer side, which is the structural reason small owners earn mid-cycle returns rather
than rents.

FY2026, the year to 30 June 2026, was the trough year. Revenue fell to IDR291.1bn from IDR365.9bn, gross profit to IDR69.8bn from IDR115.9bn, and net profit attributable to owners to IDR55.4bn from IDR95.6bn [S6, F1-F4, F12]. The gross margin fell to 24.0% from 31.7%, while general and administrative expenses were almost flat at IDR24.8bn against IDR24.8bn [S6, F5, F6]. That is the operating leverage of a fixed fleet: a revenue decline of roughly a fifth took more than a third out of gross profit. Depreciation and amortisation were IDR91.2bn, dominated by dry-dock amortisation and vessel depreciation, and the data pack's near-zero D&A is wrong; we restate it from the notes [S6, F7, F8, p.52]. EBITDA on the restated basis was IDR132.4bn [model].

The first quarter of FY2027 was weaker again. Revenue was IDR69.8bn against the prior-year quarter, gross profit IDR13.5bn, and profit for the period IDR11.4bn [S8, F20, F21, F29]. The revenue decline is consistent with the lost Kartika and Maritim Barito programmes annualising, and the gross margin of roughly a fifth is the level we anchor FY2027E to [S8]. We do not extrapolate the full quarterly decline into the year because the prior-year quarter was itself a high base, but we do not assume a second-half recovery either: FY2027E revenue is IDR279.2bn, a decline of -4.1%, and the gross margin is 20.5% [model]. FY2027E revenue holds the latest quarter's annualised run-rate rather than extrapolating its year-on-year decline, because the prior-year quarter was itself a high base and no further contract loss is disclosed [S8, F20]. The gross margin recovers to the 24.0% FY2026A level and no further: the 31.7% FY2025A level was earned on the Kartika and Maritim Barito charter volume that has since left, so that level is the bull case, not the base [S6, F1, F3, F14, F15].

Our forecast keeps the cost structure at the last actual in real terms. SG&A is held at 8.6% of revenue, in line with the FY2026 ratio and the latest quarter [S6, F5, S8]. D&A is 32.0% of revenue in FY2027E, falling to 31.0% as revenue recovers modestly, because the dry-dock schedule is fixed and does not shrink with the top line [S6 p.52]. Capex is 25.0% of revenue in FY2027E, carrying the first-quarter dock cycle, then 31.0% through the explicit period, equal to the D&A charge so that the fleet is replaced rather than consumed [S6, F7, F9, F10, p.24, S8 p.7]. The historical outlay under-replaced the depreciation charge; extrapolating it would assume the fleet shrinks, which no disclosure supports, so the base case funds replacement and carries no growth capex [S6 p.24]. Operating working capital is 17.6% of revenue, in line with the FY2026A balance-sheet ratio of IDR51.3bn on revenue of IDR291.1bn; the slow receivable from one coal customer is carried at face in that ratio and we neither release nor rebuild it [S6 p.10, p.57]. The effective tax rate is 2.0%: domestic shipping revenue pays a final tax of 1.2% of gross revenue inside operating expenses, and the residual corporate tax was negligible in FY2026 [S6 p.11, p.30, F22].

The balance sheet is the story. At 30 June 2026 the IDR504.8bn of cash and investments credited in the valuation bridge split into IDR63.4bn of cash on hand, IDR275.0bn of time deposits and IDR166.4bn of government bonds at market value [S6 p.10, p.50], against finance-lease debt of IDR0.3bn [S6 p.10]. The September balances were higher again: cash, time deposits and bond investments of IDR66.1bn, IDR276.0bn and IDR167.5bn [S8, F16-F18]. We credit the 30 June balances, so the bridge is conservative rather than stale and we do not add the increase as a second cash item. Cash and time deposits alone are below the market capitalisation; the claim that net cash exceeds it rests on counting the bond portfolio, whose maturities run from 2042 to 2049, so its market value carries duration and rate risk [S6 p.50, S0]. Equity is IDR910.2bn, of which the consolidated unappropriated balance is in deficit; the positive total comes from share capital, additional paid-in capital and a large currency-translation reserve [S6 p.10]. Return on equity was 6.3% in FY2026 after 11.9% in FY2025, which is low precisely because half the equity is liquid and earning a deposit rate [S6 p.47]. Capital allocation is conservative: no debt, no acquisition, no rights issue, and capex funded from cash [S6, S8]. Finance income was IDR20.5bn in FY2026, consistent with the deposit coupon disclosed in the notes [S6 p.11, p.47].

Earnings quality gets a mixed but not disqualifying read. The accruals screen is flattered by a working-capital release: operating working capital fell to IDR51.3bn from IDR89.0bn while revenue fell, so cash conversion in FY2026 was better than the profit line suggests [S6 p.10]. That is a one-off release, not a repeatable source of cash, and we do not capitalise it. Customer concentration is extreme: three customers, all of revenue, the largest at 41.6% [S6 p.74]. The group provides an expected-credit-loss allowance against receivables whose ageing table shows a large past-due bucket, which is the right accounting but confirms that counterparty risk is real [S6 p.47-49]. The related-party note presents key-management compensation and no related-party trade balance [S6 p.67]. There is no special-monitoring board or notation flag disclosed in the filings, and the auditor issued an unqualified opinion [S6 p.4]. We classify the customer concentration and the receivable ageing as optics-class risks that cap the multiple, not manipulation-class findings.

We value RIGS on a through-cycle FCFF DCF, weighted at 100.0%. The method set fits because the asset is a long-lived fleet with contracted cash flows and a finite economic life, and because the balance sheet is dominated by liquid instruments whose value is observable. We do not lead with EV/EBITDA or P/B, but not for the reason the arithmetic of a negative market enterprise value suggests. Net cash — cash, time deposits and the bond portfolio — exceeds the market capitalisation [S0, S6 p.10, p.50]: that says the market is pricing the operating business below zero, not that a multiple is unusable. On an ex-cash basis the operating business still has an enterprise value, and a peer EV/EBITDA multiple on FY2027E EBITDA of IDR122.6bn capitalises the charter book at a positive number which, added back to net cash, reconciles toward the DCF value rather than contradicting it [model]. The P/B leg is less useful because it would apply a fleet multiple to total equity of which more than half is cash, deposits and bonds, double-counting what the DCF already carries [S6 p.10, S8 p.4]. Both legs are therefore shown as cross-checks in the table below, not as weights.

The cost of capital is built line by line from the Indonesian sovereign curve, and every input below is a model output so the arithmetic can be reproduced [model]. The local-currency risk-free rate is 7.45%. The cash flows are in rupiah, so the build deducts the Indonesia sovereign default spread of 1.62% rather than using the dollar rate, then adds the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and the country risk premium of 2.46%, scaled by the levered beta. The unlevered beta is 1.00; re-levering it for the negligible debt-to-equity ratio of 0.00 gives a levered beta of 1.00, and the cost of equity is (7.45% − 1.62%) + 1.00 × (4.23% + 2.46%) + 0.00% = 12.52%. The pre-tax cost of debt is 9.45%, taxed at 22%, and with equity and debt weights of 99.9% and 0.1% the WACC is 99.9% × 12.52% + 0.1% × 9.45% × one minus the 22% tax rate = 12.52%. Because debt is negligible the cost of equity and the WACC agree at the second decimal, and the table below carries the same rows [model]. The terminal growth rate is 2.5%, the long-run rupiah inflation midpoint, applied after the explicit years to a business that grows with coal-logistics volume [deck]. The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR403.9bn, of which terminal value is 36.8%; adds the cash balance less debt; and gives Rp1,491 per share before the liquidity discount [model]. The twelve-month target applies the same roll-forward in every scenario: the base case grows that value at the cost of equity and subtracts next-twelve-month DPS of Rp0, giving Rp1,678; the probability-weighted scenario value is Rp1,826; and the 20.0% house discount for the thin free float takes that weighted value to the Rp1,461 target [model][S0].

The terminal cash flow is a replacement cash flow. Capex is set equal to the 31.0% D&A charge from FY2028E, so the terminal perpetuity no longer capitalises a business that under-replaces its fleet: at the historical outlay the explicit years would have spent materially less than the fleet consumes, which is the overstatement the red team identified [S6, F7, F9, F10]. Vessels and dry-dock charges are depreciated over the disclosed vessel and equipment life range and the group gives no fleet-age schedule, so a flat-volume base case must fund replacement at the depreciation rate [S6 p.24, p.52]. The change takes the enterprise value to IDR403.9bn and the target to Rp1,461.

The cash is credited at face and the 20.0% haircut is the house ADTV-based schedule, not an analyst judgment: it stands in for both the 17.5% free float and the 82.2% controller's ability to redirect the balance sheet [S0, S9]. We do not add a second trapped-cash haircut in the base case because the cash is unrestricted [S8 p.40], earns a disclosed deposit coupon [S6 p.47], and the related-party note shows no loan, guarantee or trade balance to an affiliate [S6 p.67]. We test the other side explicitly: a substantial cash haircut would take the value toward the bear case but still leave the shares above the current price, because the net cash alone is IDR504.8bn against a IDR365.5bn market value [S0, S6 p.10].

The commodity-cyclical output contract asks for a dividend-capacity anchor even where payout is zero. The unappropriated deficit was IDR69.8bn at 30 June 2026 [S6 p.10]; the model's FY2027E profit of IDR63.2bn leaves a small residual balance, which FY2028E profit then clears. The FY2028E free cash flow to equity of IDR72.5bn is therefore a post-clear run-rate, not the FY2028E distributable stream: in the transition year the remaining deficit absorbs part of it. On today's IDR365.5bn market value that run-rate is a 19.8% dividend-capacity yield, and it sits inside the DCF NAV of Rp1,491 per share [S6 p.10, model]. We keep payout at zero until an AGM approves a distribution, so the target does not capitalise that stream: it is the capacity the market is not paying for, not a forecast dividend.

The cross-checks bracket the primary value rather than contradicting it. At the Rp600 price the shares trade on 6.6x FY2026 earnings, 5.8x FY2027E earnings and 0.4x book. The reported EV/EBITDA of -1.8x is negative only because the market enterprise value subtracts the excess cash; on an ex-cash basis the operating business trades on a normal going-concern multiple, which is the same point the peer cross-check above makes [model][S0]. The FCFE yield on our FY2027E estimate is 23.2%, which is the cash return an owner would earn if the fleet simply maintained itself and the cash pile stayed put [model]. Those are not normal multiples for a going concern; they are the signature of a company whose liquid assets are worth more than its equity. The reverse DCF cannot be solved because the price is below the net-cash floor, so we state the implication directly: at Rp600 the market is assigning a negative value to the operating fleet, even though that fleet generated IDR132.4bn of EBITDA in the trough year [S6, F7].

The honest counter-argument is that a discount to net cash is not automatically value: controlled companies with thin floats can trade below cash for years, and the cash may be deployed at poor returns or never returned. We accept that. Our target already applies a 20.0% discount and does not assume any dividend. The bull case of Rp2,439 requires the charter book to recover toward FY2025 levels only; payout stays zero in every scenario. The bear case of Rp1,069 assumes further customer losses and a margin stuck at the first-quarter level [model]. The wide gap between them is the risk the red team should test.

The dominant downside is customer concentration. Three customers take all of the revenue, the largest 41.6%, and two of the three cut their charter programmes sharply in FY2026 [S6 p.74, F13-F15]. A decision by the largest customer to insource or re-let its tonnage would take the operating value toward the bear case with little warning. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high. The bear is calibrated to that event, not merely to a soft market: its growth shock is applied to every forecast year, so the shortfall compounds to a revenue base well below the base case by the terminal year, which is at least as severe as losing the largest customer's 41.6% of revenue in one step [S6 p.74, F27]. We therefore do not run a separate one-customer variant; the existing bear already contains it, and a second variant would stack two correlated shocks [model].

The second risk is the coal-volume cycle. The deck already embeds Newcastle at US$118/t for FY2027E against a spot of US$150/t, so a further fall is not in our numbers; but a sustained sub-deck price would depress Indonesian export volumes and charter rates together [deck]. The thermal-coal view is neutral and the commodity bloc is neutral, which we read as no tailwind rather than a headwind. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

The third is operational and capital intensity. Dry-dock spending is lumpy and largely non-discretionary; the first quarter of FY2027 absorbed capex equal to a large share of its revenue [S8 p.7]. A slip in the dry-dock schedule or an unplanned repair would hit revenue and cash at the same time. The fleet is old enough that maintenance is a permanent charge, not a growth investment [S6 p.52]. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

The fourth is governance and capital allocation. The controlling shareholder holds 82.2% and the free float is 17.5%, so minority holders cannot force a distribution; the cash can sit indefinitely [S0, S9]. The consolidated unappropriated balance is in deficit, which constrains dividends under Indonesian company law until profits rebuild [S6 p.10, S10 p.80]. A related-party transaction or a value-destructive diversification would be hard to resist. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

The fifth is liquidity. Average daily traded value is about IDR159.7m and the free float is 17.5% [S0]. A thin float amplifies moves in both directions and is why the house ADTV schedule applies the 20.0% discount. We make no claim about this stock's index membership or MSCI treatment beyond what the filings and the data pack support; a forced index deletion would be an added risk, not a modelled one. Likelihood: high. Impact: low to medium.

Macro and FX are the smallest risks. Receipts and costs are in rupiah, the group does not hedge, and a rupiah move of the size disclosed in the sensitivity note changes after-tax profit by a trivial amount [S6 p.71]. Brent matters through bunker fuel, but the contracts pass fuel through or have the customer supply it [S6 p.71]. A stronger rupiah would modestly reduce the reported value of the translation reserve but not the operating cash flow.

The bear case assumes the two lost programmes do not return, the largest customer trims, and the gross margin stays near the first-quarter level; it values the equity at Rp1,069. The base case reproduces FY2026 at the deck's FY2027E prices, holds costs flat in real terms and assumes no recovery in charter volume; it values the equity at Rp1,491. The bull case restores the FY2025 charter book and adds a fourth customer, operating-only with payout at zero; it values the equity at Rp2,439 [model]. The shocks are mirrored: the same two drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, move by equal and opposite amounts, and the bull margin returns to the FY2025A level while the bear takes it below the Q1 trough [model]. The output values are not symmetric, and we do not claim they are: a margin shock of equal size produces a larger equity swing on the upside because the fixed crew and dry-dock base turns a recovery into operating leverage, while the downside is cushioned by the net-cash floor. That convexity is mechanical and sourced in the cost structure, not an asymmetric haircut [S6, F5, F6]. It does not drive the call: with the bear probability doubled and the bull removed, the expected return remains strongly positive and the rating is unchanged [model].

Signposts that would change the view: a new multi-year charter with a fourth coal producer; the annual-meeting resolution on the use of FY2026 profit; a first dividend or buyback; a large related-party transaction; a step-up in the Newcastle or HBA deck; and the half-year FY2027 revenue line against the IDR69.8bn first-quarter base.

Control is concentrated and stable. PT Surya Indah Muara Pantai is the ultimate parent and holds 80.5% of the shares, a block acquired from Scomi Marine in 2022 [S10 p.18, S6 p.15, F23]. The company's shareholder page records the same controller, with the remainder held by the public as of June 2023 [S9]; the data pack's insider figure of 82.2% and free float of 17.5% are consistent with that structure after later minor changes [S0]. The board has three commissioners, one of them independent, and a small executive team; the annual meeting on 10 November 2026 will vote on a change of business classification and a change of board composition, without naming candidates in the published notice [S6 p.15, S5].

Related-party dealings appear limited. The FY2026 related-party note presents key-management compensation and does not present related-party revenue, purchase, loan or guarantee balances [S6 p.67]. The three anchor customers are third parties [S6 p.47]. We found no disclosed pledge of the controlling stake in the FY2026 financial statements; the pledges we could identify relate to bank balances, not shares [S6 p.46]. That is a clean structure flag, but it is an absence of disclosure rather than a positive assurance.

The audit is unqualified. The independent auditor's report dated 8 September 2026 states that the consolidated statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position and performance in accordance with Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S6 p.4, p.9]. The key audit matter is the carrying amount of the vessels, IDR328.7bn or roughly a third of total assets, which is the right matter to flag for a fleet owner [S6 p.5]. The statutory reserve was reduced by a transfer to unappropriated reserves at the November 2025 annual meeting, not by a dividend [S6 p.67].

The dividend record is the weak point for income investors. The company resolved not to pay a dividend at the 2021 annual meeting and has not declared one since; the FY2026 statement of changes in equity shows the only direct equity movement was that reserve transfer, and the financing cash flows in both FY2026 and FY2025 contain no dividend line [S10 p.80, S8 p.6, S6 p.78]. The pack's trailing DPS is 0.0 [S0]. We therefore carry zero dividends in the base case with that explicit basis; a first distribution is a bull-case event, not a base-case assumption. Dividend capacity exists in the cash balance, but the consolidated unappropriated account is in deficit, so a distribution requires either a profit rebuild or a capital restructuring [S6 p.10].

ESG exposure is the transition risk of coal logistics. The company earns its revenue from moving thermal coal, so it is exposed to the energy transition through its customers' volumes rather than through its own emissions; the fleet's direct emissions are a second-order issue [S6 p.70]. The company lists annual and sustainability reports on its website, including a FY2026 report, but the narrative document itself was not archived; our review relies on the audited financial statements and the website index [S2]. Social and safety risk is material for a barge operator, and the financial statements do not quantify it. Governance is family-controlled with a thin float, which the liquidity discount already reflects.

The near catalyst is the annual general meeting on 10 November 2026. The agenda covers approval of the FY2026 accounts, the use of FY2026 profit, the appointment of the FY2027 auditor, remuneration, a change of business classification under the current KBLI standard, and a change of directors and commissioners [S5]. The profit-use resolution is the first credible window for a dividend or buyback; the classification change may signal a broadening beyond coal transport, which we would treat as a new risk until the strategy is disclosed.

The operating catalysts are the quarterly reports. The half-year FY2027 results, due by the end of February 2027, will show whether the IDR69.8bn first-quarter revenue is the new run-rate or a seasonal low [S8]. We will watch revenue by customer against the FY2026 base of IDR121.0bn, IDR96.5bn and IDR73.6bn [S6, F13-F15]; the gross margin against the 20.5% FY2027E assumption; fuel and lubricants against the IDR35.1bn FY2026 base [S6, F24]; capex and dry-dock spend against the 25.0% assumption; and the cash, deposit and bond balances against the IDR504.8bn starting point [S8, F16-F18]. A new charter with a fourth customer, or the loss of one of the three, would move the thesis more than any coal-price print.

The market-level signposts are the coal deck and the macro stance. A move in Newcastle away from the US$118/t FY2027E marker, a change in the HBA reference, or a shift in the balance-of-payments stance would change the through-cycle marker we capitalise [S6]. We will re-set the marker before judging the name if the complex moves, per the commodity-cyclical method card.

bear.narrative: Coal charter demand keeps falling: Kartika and Maritim Barito, whose revenue fell 44% and 20% in FY2026 [S6, F14, F15], cut further, and the Q1 FY2027 revenue decline persists. Dry-dock amortisation and crew costs are fixed, so the gross margin stays near the Q1 trough and the fleet's utilisation falls. Newcastle stays below the deck and no new customer is signed. Net cash protects the balance sheet but does not stop the operating value from shrinking.

bull.narrative: Indonesian thermal-coal exports recover with the reviewed Newcastle path, the three anchor customers restore the FY2025 charter volumes and RIGS wins a fourth coal miner. The brent deck at USD84 lowers bunker cost, dry-dock spending normalises and the gross margin returns to the FY2025A 31.7% earned on that charter book. The bull is operating-only: the accumulated deficit and the November 2026 AGM mean a distribution is not assumed, and no payout or buyback is valued.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2027E -4.1%: the three months to 30 September 2026 delivered IDR 69.8bn [S8, F20], which annualises to IDR 279.1bn against FY2026 revenue of IDR 291.1bn [S6, F1], -4.1%; we hold the latest quarter's run-rate rather than extrapolating its -10.2% year-on-year decline, because Q1 FY2026 was itself a high base and no further contract loss is disclosed. FY2028E 0%: the three coal customers are held at the FY2027E level until the coal deck's newc path stabilises; no contract win or loss is disclosed [S6 p.57]. FY2029E to FY2031E +2.0% a year: charter rates track the reviewed Newcastle deck and Indonesian coal export volume, with no share gain assumed [coal deck]. Long-run growth 2.5%, the rupiah inflation midpoint, is applied only after the explicit period. The FY2026A collapse (-20.4%, Kartika -44% and Maritim Barito -20% [S6, F13-F15]) is the last actual and is not extrapolated.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2027E 20.5% holds the Q1 FY2027 actual, 19.3% gross profit on IDR 69.8bn [S8, F20, F21], with a small recovery through the year as the lost Kartika and Maritim Barito quarters annualise out. FY2028E 22.0% and FY2029E 23.0% return toward, but do not exceed, the FY2026A actual of 24.0% (IDR 69.8bn on IDR 291.1bn [S6, F1, F3]); the FY2025A 31.7% is not a target because it was earned on higher Kartika and Maritim Barito charter volume that has since fallen [S6, F14, F15]. From FY2030E 23.5% and FY2031E 24.0% equal the last actual; no margin expansion above it is assumed. The path is a base-input-cost margin: fuel is passed through under the contract terms in link2_pass, so the Brent deck does not move the engine's gross-margin line. Dry-dock amortisation sits inside cost of revenue, so the gross margin already carries the fleet's maintenance cycle [S6 p.52].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zero: RIGS buys no coal. Its cost of revenue is crew, fuel and lubricants, vessel depreciation, dry-dock amortisation, repairs, freight-related costs, insurance and deck supplies [S6 p.57]. The Newcastle price affects coal charter demand and rates, carried in revenue growth, not a cost line.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Zero because link1_share is zero: there is no coal-linked cost to pass through. The linkage from the coal cycle to RIGS is demand for coal-transport charters, captured in revenue growth [S6 p.57].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel and lubricants were IDR 35.1bn of FY2026 cost of revenue of IDR 221.4bn, 15.9% [S6, F24]. That is the share of the cost base exposed to Brent; there is no other material oil-linked line. We use 15.9%.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Full pass-through (1.0): fuel is bought at market price, but the LK states that the group manages the price risk by diversifying its contracts so that either the customer provides the fuel or the price charged is adjusted to current fuel prices for the service period [S6 p.71]. The group therefore does not absorb a Brent move in its gross margin; the 15.9% fuel share of cost of revenue is carried only to size the exposure, and the base-case margin path is the engine's gross-margin line without a fuel adjustment.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026A general and administrative expenses were IDR 24.8bn on revenue of IDR 291.1bn, 8.5% [S6, F1, F5]; Q1 FY2027 was IDR 6.0bn on IDR 69.8bn, 8.6% [S8]. We hold 8.6% flat: the cost base is largely fixed in rupiah (office and 42 employees [S0]) and does not fall with revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: FY2026 D&A was IDR 91.2bn, 31.3% of revenue, and FY2025 IDR 97.2bn [S6, F7, F8], not the IDR 0.83bn in the Yahoo pack. The charge is dominated by dry-dock amortisation (IDR 69.1bn FY2026) and vessel depreciation (IDR 21.3bn) [S6 p.52]. FY2027E 32.0% reflects the lower revenue base with the same dry-dock schedule; the ratio eases to 31.0% from FY2028E as revenue recovers modestly.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Replacement capex, not the historical cash outlay. FY2026 capex was IDR 49.6bn (17.0% of revenue) after IDR 87.2bn (23.8%) in FY2025 [S6, F9, F10], but D&A was IDR 91.2bn (31.3%) in FY2026 and IDR 97.2bn in FY2025 [S6, F7, F8]: for nine years the cash spend under-replaced the fleet. Vessels and dry-dock charges are depreciated over 2.5-25 years [S6 p.24], and the group gives no fleet-age schedule, so a flat-volume base case cannot assume the fleet shrinks. We therefore set capex equal to the 31% D&A charge from FY2028E (no growth capex; no fleet expansion is announced [S6, S8]). FY2027E 25% carries the Q1 FY2027 dock cycle of IDR 29.5bn [S8 p.7]. Because the engine's perpetuity capitalises FY2036E FCFF, the 31% terminal rate is already inside the terminal cash flow rather than applied separately.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2026A balance-sheet ratio. Trade receivables of IDR 50.1bn, inventories and prepayments against trade payables of IDR 5.96bn give engine operating working capital of IDR 51.3bn on FY2026 revenue of IDR 291.1bn, 17.6% [S6 p.10, p.57]. We hold 17.6% rather than extrapolate the FY2026 working-capital release: the slow receivable from one coal customer is carried at face in the ratio, and no disclosure supports either further release or a rebuild.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Domestic shipping revenue pays final tax of 1.2% of gross revenue, booked in operating expenses, on top of the engine's tax line [S6, F22, p.30]. The residual corporate income tax was IDR 0.06bn on pre-tax profit of IDR 55.4bn in FY2026 (0.1%) and IDR 5.3bn on IDR 101.0bn in FY2025 (5.3%) [S6 p.11]. Set 2.0% on pre-tax profit as the mid-point of the two years.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Debt is negligible: IDR 0.3bn at 30 June 2026 against IDR 504.8bn of cash and investments [S6 p.10]. Finance costs of IDR 20.0m on opening debt of IDR 0.57bn imply about 3.5%, but the balance is immaterial; set 8.0% to avoid a spurious low rate if any lease debt is added.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Set 6.2% on the cash, deposits and bond portfolio. The FY2026A realised yield was 5.5% (finance income IDR 20.5bn on opening cash of IDR 370.3bn [S6 p.11]), and the disclosed forward coupons support a higher rate: time deposits of IDR 275bn split between 5.50% (IDR 70bn) and 6.65% (IDR 205bn), a 6.36% blended deposit yield [S6 p.47], and government bonds at 6.875-7.375% [S6 p.50]. A 6.2% blended rate sits between the realised and contractual rates and leaves the cash sitting in demand deposits earning nothing.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: RIGS is net cash by more than its market capitalisation, with IDR 504.8bn of cash and investments against IDR 0.3bn of debt at 30 June 2026 [S6 p.10], and it funds capex from cash. No new facility, rights issue or borrowing is announced [S6, S8].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: FY2026 other expenses of IDR 6.0bn were a net foreign-exchange and sundry charge and Q1 FY2027 other income was IDR 0.9bn [S6 p.11, S8 p.5]; neither is recurring or forecastable, and asset-sale gains (IDR 0.25bn FY2026) are lumpy. No repeating item is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group has one subsidiary and no minority interest line in the FY2026 consolidated balance sheet or income statement [S6 p.10-11].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base case: the 2021 AGM resolved no dividend [S10 p.80], the FY2026 statement of changes in equity moves only by profit, OCI and a Rp10.6bn reserve transfer, and the FY2026 and FY2025 financing cash flows carry no dividend line [S6 p.78, S8 p.6]. The 10 November 2026 RUPST will decide the use of FY2026 profit [S5], but no dividend has been declared. The consolidated unappropriated balance is in deficit, which constrains a distribution under Indonesian company law until profits rebuild; a first dividend is not a base-case assumption and is shown only as dividend capacity in the report.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: 609.13m shares outstanding at 30 June 2026, unchanged over the forecast [S6 p.10, S0]. No buyback, rights issue or placement is announced [S5, S6].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: Bank Indonesia's long-run inflation target midpoint for rupiah cash flows [macro deck inflation_idr_lt], a mature coal-transport charter business growing with Indonesian coal logistics volume after the explicit years. Below the 3% historical nominal growth of the business.

challenges.challenge: The Gordon terminal value (IDR801.1bn, 37.6% of EV) is FY2036E FCFF of IDR78.3bn times 10.229, and FY2036E capex is IDR69.0bn = 22.0% of revenue while D&A is IDR97.3bn = 31.0%. The assumptions state 'Terminal capex is 31% of revenue', but the engine never applies the lt 0.31, so the perpetuity capitalises a cash flow that under-replaces the fleet by IDR28.2bn a year. At 31% terminal capex EV falls to about IDR564bn and value per share to about Rp1,755 (-6.8%), i.e. a target near Rp1,690.
challenges.answer: Correct. FY2036E was still at 22% capex, so the perpetuity capitalised a fleet that under-replaced its D&A charge. Capex is now 31% of revenue from FY2028E through FY2036E, equal to the restated D&A rate, and FY2036E therefore carries replacement capex inside the terminal cash flow that the Gordon growth capitalises. The enterprise value falls from IDR642.1bn to {{val.methods.dcf_fcff.ev}} and the target from Rp1,811 to {{val.tp_final}}. No separate terminal-capex switch exists in the engine, so the explicit-year route is the correct wiring.

challenges.challenge: Explicit capex is 22% of revenue in FY2028E-FY2036E versus D&A of 31%, a ~9pp (about IDR25bn a year) shortfall for nine years while revenue grows 0-2%. S6 note 2h gives vessel useful life of 2.5-25 years but no fleet-age schedule; the two-year capex average is 20.8% versus a 28.7% D&A average, and Q1 FY2027 capex of IDR29.5bn (about 42% annualised) points to a catch-up dock cycle. Either the fleet is being consumed (revenue overstated) or replacement capex is understated.
challenges.answer: Accepted in the direction that matters: replacement capex was understated. The LK discloses vessel and equipment lives of 2.5-25 years [S6 p.24] but no fleet-age schedule, so a flat-volume base case cannot assume the fleet shrinks. Capex is set equal to the 31% D&A charge from FY2028E (no growth capex; no fleet expansion is announced), with FY2027E at 25% to carry the IDR29.5bn Q1 dock cycle [S8 p.7]. This removes the nine-year under-replacement and the terminal under-replacement at once. We do not claim a fleet-age number the LK does not give.

challenges.challenge: The bear case shocks only revenue growth of -8pp and gross margin of -5pp. It does not model a discrete loss of a named customer, although Arutmin alone is 41.6% of revenue (IDR121.0bn) and the top three are 100%; the report itself says a largest-customer decision 'would take the operating value toward the bear case', which understates a >40% revenue event.
challenges.answer: The existing bear already contains a customer loss, indeed a larger one. The engine applies a scenario growth shock to every forecast year, so the -8pp is not a one-year event: against the base 0% then 2% path it compounds to a revenue base far below base by FY2036E, a cumulative shortfall greater than the one-off loss of the largest customer's 41.6% share. Adding a second, correlated customer-loss shock would stack the same event and breach the four-shock / mirrored-scenario house rule. We have made the reconciliation explicit in §5 instead of adding a redundant variant.

challenges.challenge: The net-cash floor (IDR504.5bn) is 44% of DCF equity value, but the model adds it at face with only a single 20% liquidity discount. The cash is unrestricted (S8 p.40) yet not distributable until the unappropriated deficit clears (FY2028 on the model's own profits), and an 80.5% controller can redirect it. No trapped-cash or control haircut, and no value-destructive related-party use, is quantified in the bear or the bridge, even though the report acknowledges the risk.
challenges.answer: The cash is unrestricted [S8 p.40] and earns a disclosed deposit coupon [S6 p.47], and the related-party note shows no loan, guarantee or trade balance to an affiliate [S6 p.67], so there is no sourced value leak to deduct in the base case. A 30% trapped-cash haircut in the base would be a default caution, which the most-likely rule forbids. The 20% house ADTV discount already stands in for the thin float and the controller's ability to redirect the balance sheet [S0, S9]; §4 now says so and notes that even a substantial cash haircut leaves the shares above the current price because net cash alone exceeds the market value. The deficit constraint is modelled through the zero payout, not through a second cash haircut.

challenges.challenge: The bull restores the FY2025 charter book (+8pp growth) and adds +5pp margin, but the resulting gross margin of about 25.5% is far below the FY2025A 31.7% earned on that same book, despite the report's own operating-leverage explanation that FY2026 compression was volume over a fixed cost base. The bull is internally inconsistent and understates the upside if volume returns.
challenges.answer: Correct: if the bull restores the FY2025 charter book it should earn the FY2025 gross margin. The bull margin shock is now +7.7pp, taking the FY2031E base margin of 24.0% to the FY2025A 31.7% earned on the same volume [S6, F3, F4]. The bear is mirrored at -7.7pp, below the Q1 FY2027 trough. Bull value rises from Rp2,912 to {{val.scenarios.bull.v0}} per share.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative says the company 'starts paying out its large net cash balance', but the bull shocks are only revenue growth and margin; payout stays zero and no dividend capacity or buyback accretion is valued. With 44% of equity in cash and shares at 0.38x book, a distribution or buyback at Rp600 is highly accretive but absent from every scenario.
challenges.answer: The inconsistency was in the narrative, not the model: the accumulated deficit constrains a distribution under Indonesian company law [S6 p.10] and no dividend has been declared [S10 p.80, S8 p.6], so a payout shock would not be the most likely path. We have removed the distribution claim from the bull narrative and state that the bull is operating-only; payout stays zero in every scenario and dividend capacity is disclosed, not capitalised. A buyback at Rp600 remains an upside we describe qualitatively rather than a modelled scenario.

challenges.challenge: The rejection of EV/EBITDA is arithmetically wrong: 'net cash exceeds the market capitalisation, so enterprise value is negative and any positive multiple produces a negative value' conflates the observed negative market EV with a valuation. Applying a peer 4.6x (BBRM 4.60, DWGL 4.62, PSSI 4.68) to FY2027E EBITDA of IDR121.8bn gives EV of IDR564bn plus net cash of IDR504.5bn, about Rp1,750 per share, which corroborates the DCF rather than contradicting it. This circularity is also why weights.changed stays unjustified.
challenges.answer: Correct, and the paragraph is rewritten. The negative market EV is a statement about the price, not a reason a multiple cannot be computed: on an ex-cash basis the operating business has a positive enterprise value, and a peer EV/EBITDA on FY2027E EBITDA of IDR121.8bn plus net cash reconciles toward, not against, the DCF. §4 now says this explicitly and describes the ex-cash P/B double-count in the right direction. weights.changed now has a sourced justification: cash is 44% of DCF equity value and is already credited in the bridge, so a P/B weight would double-count it.

challenges.challenge: The model declares link1 = d.coal.newc but link1_share = 0 and revenue is a hand-set growth path, so the coal deck has no mechanical effect on the model; the claim that FY2029E-FY2031E growth 'tracks the reviewed Newcastle deck' is not implemented. The deck's FY2027E Newcastle of 118 is 21% below spot of 150.35 and HBA is 112 versus 127, so a spot-holding scenario is untested upside.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the wording, and §2 now carries the reconciliation. RIGS buys no coal, so there is no coal-linked cost line and an elasticity into revenue would be invented rather than sourced [S6 p.57]; the deck is contextual. We state that the base grows revenue at the explicit rate and terminal growth, assumes no charter-rate re-rating above the deck's long-run marker, and treats a spot-holding Newcastle path as upside to the bull, not a base-case input. The terminal 2.5% is the macro deck's long-run rupiah inflation marker [deck], consistent with a mature nominal cash flow.

challenges.challenge: F25 (dps FY2026A = 0) quotes a reserve transfer ('Pengalihan dana... dicadangkan... 10,603,782,496'), which S6 p.67 confirms is the 5 November 2025 AGM transfer of appropriated to unappropriated reserves, not a dividend statement. The nil-DPS conclusion is genuinely evidenced elsewhere (S10 p.80: the 16 November 2021 AGM resolved no dividend; S6 p.78 and S8 p.6 show no dividend line), but the fact label and quote, and the [S0, S5, S6] basis, do not carry that evidence, and payout is set to zero for all ten years although the deficit clears by FY2028.
challenges.answer: Accepted. F25's label now states that the reserve transfer is the only direct equity movement and that nil DPS follows from the absence of any dividend charge, with the 2021 AGM resolution [S10 p.80] and the absence of a dividend line in the FY2026/FY2025 financing flows [S6 p.78] named. The payout basis now cites S10 p.80, S6 p.78 and S8 p.6, states the unappropriated-deficit constraint and that a distribution is a bull-case event; the payout stays zero for all forecast years because no AGM has approved one.

challenges.challenge: The 20.0% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted value with no source or decomposition between illiquidity and control/trapped cash. The free float is 17.5% in S0 but 19.46% is implied by S9's 80.54% controller; a plus or minus 10pp change moves the target by about 10% (Rp1,585-2,038). For an 80.5%-controlled, no-dividend issuer this is the largest judgment after the cash.
challenges.answer: The 20% is not an analyst judgment: it is the house ADTV-based schedule in fund rules applied mechanically by the engine from the measured three-month traded value [S0]. It is not decomposed because it is a prescribed haircut, not a free discount, and the engine will reproduce it for any analyst on this ADTV band. §4 now states that basis and that it stands in for both the thin float and the controller's ability to redirect cash. The target moves roughly one-for-one with a change in the rate, so we keep the house number; the doubled- bear case already shows the rating does not depend on it.

challenges.challenge: The report says the scenarios are mirrored with no asymmetric haircut, but the outputs are not mirrored: bear Rp1,542 (-27% vs base) and bull Rp3,276 (+55%), and the probability-weighted Rp2,264 exceeds the base Rp2,118 by 6.9% purely from compounding the opposite-signed growth shock. About Rp117 per share (6.4%) of the Rp1,811 target comes from that convexity.
challenges.answer: The driver shocks are now exactly mirrored: growth +/-8pp and gross margin +/-7.7pp, so the bull reaches the FY2025A margin and the bear falls below the Q1 trough by the same amount. The output values remain asymmetric and the report now says why rather than claiming otherwise: equal margin shocks produce a larger equity swing on the upside because the fixed crew and dry-dock base is operating leverage, while the downside is cushioned by the net-cash floor [S6, F5, F6]. With the bear probability doubled and the bull removed the expected return stays strongly positive and the rating is unchanged, so the convexity is transparency, not the call.

challenges.challenge: Section 7 cites S2 (a 787-character annual-report index page) for the MSCI Indonesia consultation feedback date of 2027-06-30 and the exchange free-float rule change from March 2027; S2 contains neither 'MSCI' nor 'float'. Section 5 cites [konglo] for 'not on the high-shareholding-concentration list', but no konglo pack is in this packet. The assumptions' weights_basis and extreme_call justification use a market cap of IDR356.3bn against the actual IDR365.5bn (Rp600 x 609.13m).
challenges.answer: Accepted. The unsourced MSCI/IDX catalyst has been deleted from the frontmatter, and the high-shareholding-concentration sentence has been removed from §5 because no konglo pack is in this packet. Market cap is corrected to IDR365.5bn throughout the assumptions. The valuation credits the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet cash of IDR504.8bn and §3 now states that the higher September balances are not added as a second item, so there is one cash date in the bridge.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E revenue of IDR267.8bn is 4.0% below the Q1 FY2027 annualised run-rate (IDR69.8bn x 4 = IDR279.1bn) with no source for a further decline; the report takes the direction but not the level of the latest quarter. Gross margin is capped at the FY2026A 24.0% trough for the whole forecast, and terminal growth of 2.5% sits below the house CPI of 3.28%, a real terminal decline.
challenges.answer: Revenue accepted: FY2027E growth is now -4.1%, holding the Q1 FY2027 annualised run-rate of IDR279.1bn against FY2026's IDR291.1bn, rather than extrapolating the quarter's -10.2% year-on-year decline [S8, F20]. The 24.0% gross-margin ceiling is now justified in §3: it is the FY2026A actual recovered to, and the FY2025A 31.7% required the Kartika and Maritim Barito volume that has since left, so 31.7% is the bull, not the base [S6, F1, F3, F14, F15]. On terminal growth we rebut: 2.5% is not a below-CPI haircut but the macro deck's own long-run rupiah inflation marker (the midpoint of BI's target band) [deck], applied to a mature nominal cash flow; 3.28% is the current CPI print, not the long-run marker.

challenges.challenge: Open QC FIX Q8 (load-bearing): the section 4 WACC build omits the 1.62pp sovereign default spread. It states a risk-free rate of 7.45%, a mature ERP of 4.23%, a CRP of 2.46% and an unlevered beta of 1.0006, which on the stated formula sum to 14.1%, not the 12.52% COE and WACC printed. The engine's build is correct (7.45% less 1.62% plus 1.0006 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 12.52%) and the table:wacc block renders the "Less: default spread" row, but the prose build readers are given cannot be reproduced. RMKE.JK's QC found the same class of COE reconciliation defect and raised it as a BLOCK (RMKE is in revision); treat RIGS consistently.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now discloses the full build line by line with placeholders only: risk-free {{val.coc.rf|pct2}} less the Indonesia sovereign default spread {{val.coc.default_spread|pct2}}, plus the levered beta {{val.coc.beta_levered|num2}} times (mature ERP {{val.coc.erp_mature|pct2}} + CRP {{val.coc.crp|pct2}}), giving COE {{val.coc.coe|pct2}}; and WACC as the weighted cost of equity and after-tax cost of debt, {{val.coc.wacc|pct2}}, which the engine reproduces at the second decimal. The arithmetic shown is (7.45% - 1.62%) + 1.00 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 12.52%. No assumption, input, scenario or bridge item changed, so the engine output is unchanged: BUY, target Rp1,461, expected return 143.5%. Q9's two stale qc_justification figures were refreshed to the current engine EV of IDR403.9bn and terminal-value share of 36.8% at the same time.
